overview: The map calls these territories “Lombard principalities,” but its 600 to 800 outline combines northern lands associated with the kingdom at Pavia and the southern duchies. They were not one continuous collection of equal, independent principalities. The narrative follows Lombard Italy and its local communities, with named examples beyond the map’s incomplete outline. Frankish conquest changed the northern monarchy in 774, while southern Lombard rule continued.

periods.title: Kingdom and duchies
periods.summary: Lombard rulers established a kingdom in Italy alongside powerful duchies.

periods.title: A divided political inheritance
periods.summary: The Franks took the northern monarchy; Benevento remained a Lombard center.

items.text: Lombard forces entered Italy in 568 and gradually established a kingdom centered on Pavia. Dukes governed important territories, and the southern centers of Spoleto and Benevento could act with considerable independence. Byzantine rulers still held other parts of the peninsula. Travel between Lombard regions therefore did not mean traveling through one uninterrupted country.

King Rothari issued a written collection of laws in 643. It used Latin but preserved some Lombard words. Compensation for injuries depended on the victim’s social position, so the same harm did not bring the same payment for everybody. Writing rules down made royal authority visible, while also recording the inequalities of the society.

A tiny Latin sample appears on the bronze plaque associated with King Agilulf, now in Florence’s Bargello: “VICTURIA”, meaning “victory.” The early seventh-century object shows the ruler with armed attendants and winged Victory figures. Its lettering is evidence of Latin being used to proclaim Lombard kingship, not a sentence in the spoken Lombard language.

A study of the sixth- to eighth-century cemetery at Collegno, near Turin, combined graves, ancient DNA and chemical measurements of human remains. Researchers reconstructed several related family groups and found that newcomers joined the community. The local elite developed from people with varied backgrounds. A grave’s ornaments alone cannot tell us someone’s entire identity.

At Collegno, chemical evidence suggests meals containing plant foods and animal protein, with some people eating more millet than others. Close relatives sometimes had similar dietary patterns. The researchers found no significant dietary difference between the biological sexes in their sample. These are traces of one community’s eating, rather than a menu followed throughout Lombard Italy.

Cividale, a major Lombard center in Friuli, supplies useful comparisons even where the imported outline misses it. Combs from local burials were made from animal bone and could have one or two rows of teeth. Carved bone hairpins helped hold up hair or secure a veil. Grooming left sturdy little traces after the hairstyles themselves disappeared.

Bone also became entertainment equipment. Cividale finds include six-sided dice and playing counters, while pieces interpreted as parts of a game board survive too. The museum cautiously compares some possible games with draughts. We know people had the pieces; we do not have the full rulebook or the arguments about who cheated.

Animal bones placed in some Cividale graves are interpreted as funeral food offerings, including pork, birds, sheep or goats, and shellfish. Such deposits reveal how mourners equipped the dead. They should not be treated as a shopping list showing what every family ate on an ordinary Tuesday.

At Cividale’s Gallo cemetery, women’s brooches and a weaving sword from grave 9 connect dress and textile tools with public status. The museum interprets the weaving sword as a mark of rank. A tool associated with making cloth could carry meaning beyond the workshop, much as an elaborate belt could do for a warrior.

sections.title: New uses for old buildings and knowledge

items.text: At Torba, an old defensive tower became part of a women’s religious community in the eighth century. Nuns adapted rooms for burial and prayer. The surviving painted figures belong to a building used and altered over centuries. Reusing a fortress as a monastery changed the work done there without requiring every wall to be rebuilt.

In Benevento, Duke Arechis II founded Santa Sofia around 760 and placed a convent beside it under his sister Gariperga. Surviving fresco fragments tell Christian stories, including the Annunciation and Visitation. The complex joins a ruler’s family, women’s religious leadership and painters’ skill in one place that visitors can still study.

Education also connected distant courts. Paul the Deacon taught Adelperga, the daughter of King Desiderius, and followed her to Benevento when she married Arechis II. His work as a teacher and historian helped turn remembered events into written history. This is evidence for elite learning, not proof that every child could attend a school.

Charlemagne took Pavia in 774 and ended the rule of King Desiderius. Southern Benevento followed a different path and continued as a Lombard political center. The change in the northern crown did not erase the people, laws, buildings or skills described here. The map’s shared label should not give them all one identical ending.

ending.text: The northern monarchy passed to Charlemagne in 774. Benevento’s Lombard rulers survived in the south, so this broad map category has no single disappearance date. Its 800 endpoint is a change in the imported map labels.
